summary: This government bill creates a stand-alone law for the Sovereign Development Fund, a state fund meant to help repay the state's foreign debt and to cover economic crises. The fund would become a separate legal body, and the money in the existing fund under Article 30-1 of the Public Finance Act (Law No. 3/2006) would move into it; that article would then be repealed. The bill lists the money paid into the fund and limits its use to repaying debt the public bank account cannot cover and budget support after an unusual economic shock, with the President's approval on the governing council's advice. It sets up a 7-member governing council chaired by the Finance Minister, a 5-member investment committee chaired by the Accountant General, and a Sovereign Development Fund Administration Office under the Finance Ministry led by a chief executive officer. It also sets rules for audits, public reports and closing the fund.
whyItMatters: The law would decide how some state income, such as airport development fees and part of state company dividends, is saved and invested to pay off foreign debt, and who controls and checks that money.
keyProvisions: Articles 3 and 4: the fund becomes an independent legal body kept apart from the public bank account, takes over all money in the fund set up under Article 30-1 of the Public Finance Act, and exists to keep the state able to repay foreign debt, hold foreign currency for debt payments, and provide money in economic crises.

Article 5: money paid in includes airport development fees, 10% of dividend income the state gets from companies it holds shares in, sovereign guarantee fees, and other money the President sets on the governing council's advice.

Articles 6 to 8: fund money can be used only to repay debt when the public bank account cannot, or for budget support after an unusual economic shock, with the President's approval on the council's advice. All fund spending must be in the state budget. Once the fund reaches the target size set by the President, extra money goes to the budget, and lowering that target needs the People's Majlis' approval.

Articles 9 to 16: the President appoints a 7-member governing council within 30 days, chaired by the Finance Minister and including 2 senior Finance Ministry staff, the Maldives Monetary Authority Governor and a senior MMA official, a senior official of the economic ministry, and one public member chosen through an open call. Non-ex-officio members serve 5-year terms and the council meets at least 4 times a year.

Articles 17 to 31: a 5-member investment committee (the Accountant General, two senior Finance Ministry officials and two investment experts chosen through an open call) invests the fund under a policy the council approves and meets at least 12 times a year. An administration office under the Finance Ministry runs the fund, and the Maldives Monetary Authority acts as custodian.

Articles 32 to 40: the CEO reports to the council every 3 months and publishes an annual report within 4 months of each year's end, the Auditor General audits the fund every year for the Majlis committee, audit reports are published, and the fund can be closed only with the Majlis' approval, with its assets going to the state budget. The law takes effect 3 months after it is published in the Government Gazette.
whoIsAffected: The Finance Ministry, the Maldives Monetary Authority, the Accountant General and Auditor General, state-owned companies that pay dividends, and taxpayers who carry the state's debt.
statedReasons: The government says the bill sets up a Sovereign Development Fund to reduce state debt and pass the state's wealth on to future generations, sets the rules for running the fund, and sets out the duties of the state bodies connected to it.
